week_headline: India's food regulator FSSAI puts health supplement brands on notice over misleading labels, sparking wider debate about supplement industry accountability

claims.verdict: FSSAI's warnings are real and well-documented — the regulator has repeatedly flagged supplement brands for overstating benefits, hiding ingredient quantities, and using unapproved health claims on packaging. That said, the story is less about a dramatic crackdown and more about an ongoing, slow-moving regulatory tussle. The supplement industry in India operates in a genuinely grey zone where enforcement has historically been patchy, so the warnings carry weight but their follow-through is what actually matters.
claims.verdict_highlight: Labels overpromise; enforcement is the real test
sources: EFSA (European Food Safety Authority) supplement labelling standards
Journal of Nutrition — review of supplement label accuracy studies
claims.global_opinion: In the EU, EFSA maintains a strict approved-claims list meaning supplement makers cannot print health benefits without pre-authorised scientific backing — a standard India is still moving toward. The US FDA takes a post-market approach, meaning products can launch freely but face action after complaints, which critics argue lets misleading labels circulate too long. Australia's TGA sits somewhere in between, requiring pre-approval for therapeutic claims, which has generally kept its supplement market more tightly labelled than India's current framework.
claims.brit_take: In the UK, the FSA quietly does a version of this every few months and nobody really notices — until someone finds 'supports your immune system' on a gummy bear and wonders what that actually means.
claims.claim: FSSAI warns health supplement makers over labelling violations , threatens action
